description: Cases for the rule that a variable exists because it was declared. Covers a write to an undeclared name, an operation the declared type cannot take, two scripts declaring one global name incompatibly, and what clear and reset each write. Clear empties a variable for its declared type; reset puts back the value its declaration gives it. Both answer from the declaration rather than from whatever the variable happens to hold, so a case is only useful when the declared value differs from the empty one. A hotkey has no empty value, so clear has no answer for one.

clearAndReset.name: boolean
clearAndReset.reason: clear and reset agree only when the declared value is already the empty one; here they differ because the declaration says true

clearAndReset.name: color
clearAndReset.reason: a color is a JSON string, so clearing by the stored value's shape would empty it to "" instead of black

clearAndReset.name: hotkey
clearAndReset.reason: no key combination means "no key", so clear has no answer; a null clear means the operation is refused

undeclaredWrites.name: a write with no declaration at all
undeclaredWrites.reason: a declaration is what makes a variable exist, so there is nothing to write to

undeclaredWrites.name: a write to a different name than the one declared
undeclaredWrites.reason: a near miss is the typo this rule exists to catch

undeclaredWrites.name: several nodes writing one declaration
undeclaredWrites.reason: one declaration serves every node that writes it; N nodes are not N declarations

operationTypeAgreement.name: toggle a string
operationTypeAgreement.reason: the operation implies boolean and the declaration says string

operationTypeAgreement.name: increment a list
operationTypeAgreement.reason: increment pins no numeric type, so the mismatch surfaces when the value is read rather than at run start; the package loader refuses it at install

operationTypeAgreement.name: increment a float
operationTypeAgreement.reason: increment pins no numeric type and preserves the declared one

globalDeclarationConflicts.name: same name, different type
globalDeclarationConflicts.reason: a global is shared by name, so two types describe one stored value two incompatible ways

globalDeclarationConflicts.name: same name, different list item type
globalDeclarationConflicts.reason: what a list holds is part of what the value is

globalDeclarationConflicts.name: same name, same type
globalDeclarationConflicts.reason: agreeing declarations share the value, which is the point of a global

globalDeclarationConflicts.name: same name in different scopes
globalDeclarationConflicts.reason: a persistent variable belongs to one script, so two scripts naming one do not collide

refusedAtNote: undeclaredWrites and operationTypeAgreement are both package faults: the run is refused before any node executes, rather than letting a node take its failed output. A package carrying either is also refused when it is loaded.
